extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners prosecuting software- and computer-related patent applications before the USPTO/PTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and prosecuting software/computer-related patent claims to survive 35 U.S.C. § 101 subject-matter eligibility rejections, summarizing PTAB decisions and practical claim/specification drafting tips under the USPTO 2019 SME Guidance and the Alice/Mayo framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid method steps that are human cognitive actions/mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Review your method claims to determine if they can include steps that cannot be performed as "human cognitive actions" or mental process steps; if possible, include system claims that do not mirror the process steps of the method claims, and include components that can be supported as not being "standard components".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where method steps are plausibly performable mentally, amend claims to add non-mental limitations or add system/hardware claims that do not merely mirror the method steps. Support in the specification that method steps include limitations representing a specific application under the USPTO 2019 Examination Guidelines and an inventive concept that transforms the process into substantially more (so as to avoid Verified Voter-style §101 issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate abstract mental processes into a practical application (Step 2A, prong 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that "integrate the abstract mental process into a practical application" — e.g., "laying layer over an image provides a 2-dimensional graphical interface including an image, by which a user can position a pointing and selecting device over the image and quickly and easily provide evaluation of the image in two criteria simultaneously by positioning an onscreen cursor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that claim limitations provide a specific technological improvement over prior GUIs or other technology (immediate visual numerical feedback, image map with x/y coordinates, simultaneous update during user motion). If Step 2A prong 2 is met, the Board may not reach step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not draft claims that merely 'collect information, analyze it, and display certain results'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely recite collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying results are likely recited as mental processes under Step 2A, prong 1 (example language: "collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying certain results" or "judgment of the user which pertains to [a] mental process").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims include such limitations, add additional limitations that tie the steps to a technological implementation (e.g., specific UI behavior, hardware actions) or otherwise transform the claim into a 'practical application.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie claims to specific technical problems and technical-field concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail within claims tying the claims to specific problems or concepts in the given technical field can help survive §101 challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claim limitations that explicitly address the technical problem and recite the technical solution; include claim detail that ties the elements to that technical field (e.g., memory footprint/segmenting for PDF print jobs, vehicle transaction processing specifics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim specific technological improvements to underlying technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite improvements to technology (e.g., "improved computer functionality," "improvement to the operation of the insulin pump," dynamic splitting of PDF print jobs) are more likely to be treated as integrated into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize how the claimed features improve the underlying technology (reduced memory footprint, enabling vehicle transactions via dynamic UI, downloading pump configuration and delivering insulin). Support each asserted improvement in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reciting components in generic terms (show elements are non-conventional)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification describes the computer and elements in generic terms, the PTAB concluded those components were conventional computer components under Alice Step 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, claim and describe components with specificity or unconventional functionality; provide specification support that components are not "well-understood, routine, conventional activities" to avoid Step 2B rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include claim limitations that cannot practically be performed mentally
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can, explain in the specification or in a response to a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 why the claimed subject matter cannot practically be performed mentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly argue and provide factual/specification support showing that claimed processing, interactions, or hardware control steps require machine execution and are not amenable to being performed in the human mind or with pen-and-paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tangible device control or real-world effects to support practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations such as "downloading the pump configuration file from the configuration device to an insulin pump; and delivering insulin, by the insulin pump" were found to integrate an abstract idea into a practical application because they improve device operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include claim steps that cause physical or device-level effects (actuating pumps, controlling hardware, producing machine-readable ballots) and show in the specification how these steps improve operation or safety of the device/technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with 'computer-readable medium' claims that broadly cover propagation signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to a computer readable medium which broadly recite a signal and as such is not one of the four categories of patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 can be rejected (e.g., propagation signal issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming computer-readable media in a manner that could be interpreted to cover signals or propagation ineligible subject matter; define storage mediums and exclude transitory signals where appropriate in view of §101 jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft a variety of differently scoped claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A variety of differently scoped claims can provide options on appeal or challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include narrower and broader claim sets (method, system, apparatus, computer-readable medium with careful drafting) to preserve fallback positions during prosecution or appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the USPTO 2019 SME Guidance process when a judicial exception is recited
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites a judicial exception, determine whether additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A, prong 2) or whether the claim adds a specific limitation beyond the judicial exception or simply appends well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the two-prong Step 2A analysis: (1) identify whether the claim recites a judicial exception (mental process, mathematical concept, etc.); (2) evaluate whether additional claim elements integrate that exception into a practical application. If not integrated, proceed to Step 2B to evaluate inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize the claim 'as a whole' focusing on technical aspects and asserted improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board focused on the technical aspects of the claim and considering the claim as a whole (e.g., distinguishing sales/marketing behavior from a technical improvement in a print-server or search-engine use case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting/specifying, present the claim as a whole with emphasis on technical improvements and avoid framing the invention as merely a business method; explain how the combination of elements yields a technical benefit rooted in computer technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add technology to business-method claims and use non-conventional terminology where useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Add technology to your business method in order to have a chance to get it allowed. Use unconventional names, such a "proactive search engine" to make it harder to assert that the elements are conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce specific technological components or behavior that solve a technical problem; while naming alone is not sufficient, unconventional terminology combined with specification support can help distinguish claimed features from conventional systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify limitations that are indicative vs not indicative of 'integration into a practical application'
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB summarizes USPTO 2019 SME Guidance for "limitations that are indicative of 'integration into a practical application' versus limitations that are not."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or arguing eligibility, explicitly map claim limitations to the indicia in the USPTO guidance (e.g., particular machine, particular transformation, improvement to another technology, specific rules applied to a particular content) and show why each limitation is indicative of integration rather than being an abstract idea or insignificant post-solution activity.
